title: When Performing, Never Tell Yourself What Not to Do
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post is about the instructions leaders give themselves in high-pressure moments of performance. The author argues that negatively framed self-talk, such as don't drive too close to the curb, backfires because the mind fixes on exactly what it is told, in this case the curb. The common myth that the brain cannot tell do from don't is rejected; the real problem is that the brain follows the stated focus too faithfully. Top performers therefore phrase their inner voice in terms of what they intend, using forms like I intend to or I plan to, and they steer attention away from what they fear. The post closes with a sports psychologist's reminder to be careful what you say to yourself because you are listening.
points: Telling yourself what not to do tends to produce the very outcome you wanted to avoid, because attention goes to the forbidden thing.
The author corrects a myth: the brain understands negation, but it still concentrates on whatever the inner voice names.
The practical habit is positive, intention-based self-talk such as I intend to, I want to or I plan to.
Attention should be diverted from fears and placed on the desired action to support high-level execution.
quotes: Anytime a performer plants the idea of what not to do in the mind, the brain has a funny way of punishing the thought. Whatever we tell ourselves not to do usually results in the opposite outcome.
A common myth is that the brain can’t interpret the difference between do and don’t do. But here’s the truth: Telling yourself what not to do usually results in disaster.
The problem isn’t that your mind can’t distinguish between do and don’t. The issue is that your brain is too good. It focuses on exactly what you tell it to.
Top performers train themselves to always say what they want to happen. They make zero reference to what they want to avoid. As a rule, they never tell themselves what they don’t want to do.
Unfortunately, it is often more natural to focus on trouble or concern and to tell yourself to avoid it. As soon as we fall into that trap, the jaws spring tight.

How you talk to yourself and the thoughts you concentrate on have a tremendous influence on what happens during performance. In the words of one sports psychologist, you must be extremely careful about what you say to yourself because someone very important is listening — You!
